t: Find the Kth Smallest Sum of a Matrix With Sorted Rows
o: We must pick exactly one element per row; each such pick yields a sum, and we want the k-th smallest possible sum among all $n^m$ combinations. In Example 1 the smallest sums are built greedily: start with [1,2]=3, then swap one coordinate at a time ([1,4]=5, [3,2]=5, [3,4]=7, [1,6]=7), so the 5th is 7. Constraints are small ($m,n \le 40$, $k \le 200$): we never need more than the k smallest partial combinations at any point, so we can process rows one at a time and discard everything beyond rank k. This suggests either a heap-based incremental merge or a binary search on the answer value with a counting predicate.
k: After merging any prefix of rows we only need to keep the k smallest sums; larger ones can never become part of the final top-k because all future additions are non-negative.
Merging two sorted lists of candidate sums with a min-heap takes O(k log k), so folding rows in one by one costs O(m * k * n log k).
The predicate 'number of combinations with sum <= x' is monotone in x, enabling binary search on the answer over the range [sum of row minimums, sum of row maximums].

a.n: Approach 1: Row-by-row merge with a Min-Heap
a.i: Treat the problem as repeatedly merging sorted lists. Start with the first row's elements as the current set of k smallest sums. For each next row, every new sum is (previous sum + element of this row); the smallest candidates come from pairing the smallest previous sums with the smallest row elements. Use a min-heap seeded with prev[0] + row[j] for each j, pop up to k times, and each pop of (s, j) pushes s - row[j] + row[j+1] (advancing the pointer within the row) — exactly like merging k sorted lists. After processing all rows, the heap's top after popping k-1 items is the answer.
s: Initialize a list `prev` containing just 0 (empty combination sum).
For each row, build candidate sums prev[i] + row[j]; conceptually these form n sorted lists (one per j), each sorted because prev is sorted ascending.
Use a min-heap of tuples (prev[i] + row[j], i, j); push (prev[0] + row[j], 0, j) for all j.
Pop the smallest up to k times; each time you pop (s, i, j), push (prev[i+1] + row[j], i+1, j) if it exists.
Collect popped values into the new `prev` list (truncate to k) and continue; after the last row return the k-th popped value.
a.t: O(m * k * n log(k*n)) — for each of m rows we perform up to k pops/pushes on a heap of size n.
a.sp: O(k + n) — the kept sums list has at most k entries and the heap holds at most n entries.

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on the Answer with Counting DFS
a.i: Instead of enumerating sums, binary search the answer value x in [minSum, maxSum]. Define count(x) = number of one-element-per-row choices whose sum is <= x; this is non-decreasing in x, so the k-th smallest sum is the smallest x with count(x) >= k. Compute count(x) with a pruned DFS over rows: for row i try each element v <= remaining budget and recurse; stop expanding once the running count reaches k (we never need to distinguish counts above k). Sorted rows let us break out of the inner loop as soon as v exceeds the remaining budget.
s: Set lo = sum of mat[i][0] over all rows, hi = sum of mat[i][last] over all rows.
While lo < hi, set mid = (lo + hi) / 2.
Run count(mid) via DFS: at row index i with remaining budget r, if i == m return 1; otherwise iterate v over row i while v <= r, adding recursive results, aborting early once the total reaches k.
If count(mid) >= k, set hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1.
a.t: O(m * n * k * log(sumRange)) in practice — each binary search step runs a DFS that terminates after generating about k successful branches thanks to early cutoff; the search range spans at most 40*5000 = 200000, so ~18 iterations.
a.sp: O(m) recursion depth for the DFS, plus O(1) extra space.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it directly exploits 'rows are sorted', is easy to explain as repeated k-way list merging, and comfortably fits the constraints ($m \le 40$, $k \le 200$). Mention Approach 2 as an optimization when k or dimensions grow, since its cost scales with log(range) rather than with enumeration. Pitfalls: forgetting to truncate intermediate sums to the k smallest (memory/time blowup), off-by-one when returning the k-th element (index k-1), and integer overflow of sums in C++/Java (use long during binary search). Edge cases: a single row (answer is simply mat[0][k-1]), k equal to the total number of combinations, and duplicate values across rows. Likely follow-ups: handle negative numbers (breaks the sorted-list merge pruning but binary search still works), or return the actual combination rather than just the sum.
